final_answer:
>>> Antibiotic resistance arises through evolutionary mechanisms rooted in natural selection. Bacteria, which reproduce rapidly, naturally accumulate genetic mutations. When exposed to antibiotics, these drugs kill susceptible bacteria, but any resistant mutants (due to prior mutations or gene transfer) survive. These resistant bacteria then proliferate, passing on their resistance traits to subsequent generations. Over time, this leads to the dominance of antibiotic-resistant strains in the population.  

>>> Overprescription of antibiotics accelerates this process by intensifying selective pressure. Frequent or inappropriate use of antibiotics—such as prescribing them for viral infections or incomplete courses—exposes bacteria to sublethal doses. This allows resistant strains to thrive while non-resistant bacteria are eliminated. Additionally, overuse in agriculture or improper disposal of antibiotics can create environments where resistance genes spread via horizontal gene transfer (e.g., through plasmids), enabling non-resistant bacteria to acquire resistance traits rapidly. Thus, overprescription directly fuels the evolution and proliferation of antibiotic-resistant pathogens.
